summary.text: For an even \(m\) with \(m/2>6\), a witness at \(m/2\) supplies primes \(m/2-k\) and \(m/2+k\), whose sum is \(m\); the remaining cases \(m=4,6,8,10,12\) are handled by explicit prime decompositions. For odd \(N\ge9\), applying the hypothesis to the even number \(n=N-1\) gives a prime \(p\) and a prime \(n-(2p-1)\), so \(N=[n-(2p-1)]+2p\), while \(N=7\) is handled as \(3+2\cdot2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\varepsilon(n)=
\begin{cases}
1,&n\text{ odd},\\
2,&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A261627(n)\) counts the primes \(p<n+1\) for which, on putting
\[
k=p\varepsilon(n)-1,
\]
one has \(k<n\) and both
\[
n-k\qquad\text{and}\qquad n+k
\]
prime. (The condition \(k<n\) in particular ensures that the subtraction is ordinary nonnegative integer subtraction.) Assume the A261627 positivity conjecture:
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>6.
\]
We prove both asserted consequences.

First record the immediate consequence of positivity that will be used twice. If \(n>6\), then the finite set counted by \(a(n)\) is nonempty. Consequently there is a prime \(p\) such that, with
\[
k=p\varepsilon(n)-1,
\]
we have
\[
k<n,\qquad n-k\text{ is prime},\qquad n+k\text{ is prime}. \tag{1}
\]
The upper bound \(p<n+1\), which is also part of membership in the set being counted, will not be needed below.

## Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(m\ge 4\) be even. We must express \(m\) as a sum of two primes.

Suppose first that
\[
\frac m2>6.
\]
Set \(n=m/2\). By (1), there are a prime \(p\) and an integer
\[
k=p\varepsilon(n)-1<n
\]
such that \(n-k\) and \(n+k\) are prime. Since \(k<n\), no truncation is involved in \(n-k\), and therefore
\[
(n-k)+(n+k)=2n.
\]
Because \(m\) is even and \(n=m/2\), we have \(2n=m\). Hence
\[
m=(n-k)+(n+k)
\]
is a sum of two primes.

It remains to consider the case \(m/2\le 6\). Since \(m\ge4\) and \(m\) is even, the only possibilities are
\[
m\in\{4,6,8,10,12\}.
\]
Each has the required explicit decomposition:
\[
4=2+2,
\qquad 6=3+3,
\qquad 8=3+5,
\qquad 10=5+5,
\qquad 12=5+7.
\]
All numbers appearing as summands here are prime. Thus every even integer at least \(4\) is a sum of two primes, proving the strong Goldbach conjecture in the stated form.

## Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(N\ge7\) be odd. We must find primes \(r,q\) such that
\[
N=r+2q.
\]

If \(N=7\), then
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\]
and both \(3\) and \(2\) are prime.

Now suppose \(N>7\). Since \(N\) is odd, this implies \(N\ge9\). Put
\[
n=N-1.
\]
Then \(n\) is even, and \(n\ge8\), so in particular \(n>6\). Apply (1) to this \(n\). Because \(n\) is even, \(\varepsilon(n)=2\). We therefore obtain a prime \(q\) such that
\[
k=2q-1<n
\]
and, in particular,
\[
r:=n-(2q-1)
\]
is prime. (The other prime \(n+(2q-1)\) supplied by (1) is not needed for this implication.)

It remains only to check the required identity. A prime natural number is at least \(2\), so \(q\ge2\), and hence \(2q-1\) is positive and \((2q-1)+1=2q\). Since \(2q-1<n\), subtraction is exact, and thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
r+2q
  &=\bigl(n-(2q-1)\bigr)+2q\\
  &=\bigl(n-(2q-1)\bigr)+(2q-1)+1\\
  &=n+1\\
  &=N.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both \(r\) and \(q\) are prime, so this is a Lemoine representation of \(N\).

We have proved that the positivity assertion \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>6\) implies both Goldbach's conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.
